children: TOKYO-The Bank of Japan lifted its benchmark interest rate to its highest level in 30 years and signaled more increases are on the way, a policy shift with the potential for big ripples far beyond Japan's shores.
Japanese investors own around $2.5 trillion of U.S. stocks, bonds and other financial assets, accounting for about half of Japan's enormous $5 trillion stock of overseas portfolio holdings.

As rates rise, the prospect of juicier returns at home might lure some of that money back to Japan, slowing or even reversing what has been a reliable stream of cash helping prop up prices in U.S. and other global markets.
"The yen supertanker is turning," said Rory Green, head of Asia and emerging markets research at GlobalData TS Lombard in London.
The BOJ said Friday it raised its benchmark interest rate to 1.25%.

The decision follows a rate increase by the Federal Reserve on Wednesday, as well as an unusually public campaign by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent urging Japan to raise borrowing costs. Other central banks are expected to follow suit as the war in Iran squeezes energy supplies and fuels inflation.

The moves come amid surging bond yields around the world. The yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury note recently hit 5%. In Japan, 10-year yields are around 3%, a level not seen since the mid-1990s. Rising yields reflect investor anxiety about inflation and government, though also some optimism about artificial intelligence and how it might transform economic growth.

Low rates in Japan meant that Japanese investors for years looked overseas for better returns, vacuuming up U.S. Treasurys and European government bonds, as well as stocks, corporate debt and other assets. Japanese banks borrowed cheaply at home to lend overseas, pocketing the difference in yield.

Japan's Government Pension Investment Fund, which manages more than $2 trillion on behalf of Japanese workers, used to park around 60% of its assets in Japanese government bonds. More than a decade ago, it began shifting into foreign debt and equities, and today domestic Japanese bonds account for about a quarter of its portfolio.

To hit return targets, "they realized they needed more of an allocation to equities," said Eiji Ueda, who was chief investment officer at GPIF from 2020 to 2025 and is now head of Asia-Pacific at Apollo Global Management in Tokyo.
GPIF owns around $240 billion of U.S. government bonds, according to recent financial statements. Its biggest foreign equity holdings are Nvidia, Apple and Microsoft.

Japan's finance minister, Satsuki Katayama, has said she would like to see GPIF invest more of its assets at home, though government officials who oversee the fund have said no new decisions have been made.

For the U.S., Japanese investors souring on Treasurys would add to upward pressure on yields, which move inversely to bond prices. In conducting a rare joint intervention with Tokyo to prop up the yen, Bessent said that in the future, Japan should consider borrowing dollars from the Fed rather than selling down its Treasury holdings.

Japan is the largest holder of U.S. Treasurys, according to Treasury data, with around $1.1 trillion invested as of the end of July. That is down from a peak of $1.2 trillion in February, before Japan's efforts to prop up the yen.

Analysts and investors caution that any redirection of Japanese capital will be gradual and contingent on the BOJ following through with further rate increases despite pockets of weakness in the economy.

Gently rising rates in Japan might also not be enough to tempt Japanese investors to bring that much money home when they could put it in American tech stocks or pick up higher yields on other countries' bonds, which are still above those in Japan, some analysts say.

"At this point, I'm not expecting a huge repatriation of money coming from U.S. Treasurys to Japan," said Norihiro Yamaguchi, lead Japan economist at Oxford Economics in Tokyo. He said it would take more clarity on how high the BOJ intends to take its benchmark interest rate to spur Japanese investors to shift more into domestic assets.
